metadata.title: Predicting Key Factors Influencing Students’ Creative Thinking: A Machine Learning Analysis Based on PISA 2022 Data from East Asia

survey_design.weight_variable_name: SENWT (overall East Asia) and W_FSTUWT (five-economy analyses)
survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for five East Asian economies (Singapore, South Korea, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong (China), and Macao (China)) and applies complex-sampling weights to better reflect the target populations. Specifically, SENWT is used for analyses of the pooled East Asia dataset, while W_FSTUWT is used when running the separate models for each of the five economies. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation is not described at the replicate level. The analytic sample is restricted to the variables included in the socio-ecological predictor set and the dependent creative thinking score; no additional filtering rules (e.g., exclusions for missing questionnaire items) are explicitly documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is creative thinking performance, and the paper states that it uses the average of the 10 plausible values. However, the manuscript does not describe how missing questionnaire/test responses were handled before fitting LASSO and Random Forest (e.g., whether cases with missing predictors were excluded or imputed). Given that PISA background questionnaires typically contain item nonresponse, this omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect model stability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis focuses on PISA 2022 creative thinking for five East Asian economies (Singapore, South Korea, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong (China), and Macao (China)). The dependent variable is the creative thinking total score (0–60) operationalized as the average of the 10 plausible values. Predictors are restricted to the socio-ecological set of questionnaire-derived indices/scales/composites (10 individual, 8 microsystem, 8 mesosystem variables) as listed in Appendix Table 1; the paper does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., minimum item completion) or explicit missing-data rules beyond using the available dataset for these variables.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (East Asia pooled; 15-year-old students)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking performance (average of 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (17 LASSO-selected predictors) — RMSE: 8.3413; R²: 0.3414; 10-fold cross-validation; variable importance ranked by %IncMSE (ESCS highest; students’ age lowest).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for the pooled East Asia sample, the study leveraged Index of ESCS, self-efficacy in digital competencies, curiosity, ICT resources, and imagination to predict creative thinking performance, finding that ESCS was the most important predictor and the Random Forest model achieved RMSE = 8.3413 and R² = 0.3414 under 10-fold cross-validation. This indicates that strengthening students’ digital self-efficacy and curiosity—alongside reducing socioeconomic disadvantages—may be a practical route to improving creative thinking outcomes, though the results are predictive associations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking performance (average of 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (economy-specific LASSO-selected predictors) — R²: 0.3649; 10-fold cross-validation; top predictors ranked by %IncMSE (ESCS highest; school size among top three).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for Singapore, the study leveraged Index of ESCS, self-efficacy in digital competencies, and school size to predict creative thinking performance, finding that the Random Forest model reached R² = 0.3649 and that ESCS and digital self-efficacy were among the top predictors. This indicates that Singapore’s creative outcomes may be supported by socioeconomic resources and digital-competence beliefs, suggesting that policy should pair equity-oriented supports with digital learning environments that build students’ confidence to use technology creatively.

main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking performance (average of 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (economy-specific LASSO-selected predictors) — R²: 0.2241; 10-fold cross-validation; top predictors ranked by %IncMSE (ESCS highest; curiosity and imagination among top three).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for South Korea, the study leveraged Index of ESCS, curiosity, and imagination to predict creative thinking performance, finding that the Random Forest model achieved R² = 0.2241 and that ESCS, curiosity, and imagination were the leading predictors. This indicates that creative thinking in this context is more strongly tied to individual motivational/cognitive dispositions and socioeconomic background than to the measured school-level supports, implying that education policy may need to more explicitly institutionalize creativity-oriented learning experiences beyond exam-focused schooling.

main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking performance (average of 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (economy-specific LASSO-selected predictors) — R²: 0.3194; 10-fold cross-validation; top predictors ranked by %IncMSE (digital self-efficacy highest; ESCS second; class size third).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for Chinese Taipei, the study leveraged self-efficacy in digital competencies, Index of ESCS, and class size to predict creative thinking performance, finding that the Random Forest model reached R² = 0.3194 with digital self-efficacy as the strongest predictor. This indicates that policies that build students’ confidence and competence in digital environments may be especially effective for fostering creative thinking in Chinese Taipei, while also recognizing that socioeconomic resources remain a key enabling factor.

main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking performance (average of 10 plausible values)
top_predictors: Participation in creative activities outside of school
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (economy-specific LASSO-selected predictors) — R²: 0.2887; 10-fold cross-validation; top predictors ranked by %IncMSE (school size highest; ESCS second; outside-of-school creative activities among top three).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for Hong Kong (China), the study leveraged school size, Index of ESCS, and participation in creative activities outside of school to predict creative thinking performance, finding that the Random Forest model achieved R² = 0.2887 and that school size and socioeconomic status were central predictors. This indicates that scaling or resourcing school-level capacity (and ensuring that out-of-school creative activities are high-quality rather than merely time-consuming) may help improve creative thinking, though the study’s cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking performance (average of 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (economy-specific LASSO-selected predictors) — R²: 0.3656; 10-fold cross-validation; top predictors ranked by %IncMSE (school size highest; digital self-efficacy and ESCS among top three).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data for Macao (China), the study leveraged school size, self-efficacy in digital competencies, and Index of ESCS to predict creative thinking performance, finding that the Random Forest model achieved R² = 0.3656 and that school-level capacity together with digital self-efficacy and socioeconomic status were the most influential predictors. This indicates that strengthening school resources and digital learning supports may be a particularly promising policy combination for improving creative thinking in Macao, while noting that the reported relationships are predictive rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 creative thinking for five East Asian economies (SGP, KOR, TWN, HKG, MAC; total N = 29,208) using a two-stage machine learning pipeline. The dependent variable is creative thinking performance (0–60) operationalized as the average of the 10 plausible values. For the pooled East Asia sample, LASSO selects a parsimonious set of predictors and a Random Forest regression model (10-fold cross-validation) yields RMSE = 8.3413 and R² = 0.3414, with ESCS ranked as the most important predictor (by %IncMSE). Across economies, R² ranges from 0.2241 (South Korea) to 0.3656 (Macao), and the top predictors differ by context (e.g., digital self-efficacy in Chinese Taipei; school size in Hong Kong and Macao). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy for predictors, and the authors explicitly frame results as predictive correlations rather than causal effects.
